name: Strait of Hormuz crisis and Gulf tanker war
started: 2026-02-28 (Iranian closure; current phase since 2026-07-08 collapse of the Islamabad Memorandum)
summary: Since 28 February 2026 Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed with fast boats, mines, missiles, drones, jamming and seizures, letting through only ships it approves and charging tolls. The US answered with its own blockade of Iranian ports, strikes on the IRGC Navy and mine clearance. October 2026 is the most violent month for shipping since March, with mine strikes on supertankers and sinkings, and traffic down from about 85 ships a day to a handful.

sides.name: Iran
members: IRGC Navy (fast attack craft, mines, drone boats, anti-ship missiles)
IRGC Aerospace Force (ballistic and cruise missiles, drones)
Persian Gulf Strait Authority (transit permits and tolls, from 5 May 2026)
backers: China (ships with Chinese owners given passage; toll payments reportedly assessed in yuan)
leaders: Mohsen Rezaei (head of Supreme National Security Council, announced 6 Sep prohibited zone)
Alireza Tangsiri (IRGC Navy commander, reported killed Mar 2026)
sides.strength: 500 to 1,000+ fast attack boats cited (Wikipedia, 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis); 100+ suspected mines found in the Traffic Separation Scheme by Aug 2026

sides.name: United States and partners
members: US Navy and CENTCOM (blockade of Iranian ports, mine clearance, Operation Project Freedom escorts)
Indian Navy (Operations Sankalp and Urja Suraksha escorts)
Gulf states' navies and air defences
backers: Oman (offered transit through its waters; mediates with Iran)
sides.strength: US blockade in force 13 Apr to 29 May and again from about 14 Jul 2026; 15 ships seized by late July

background: About 20 million barrels of oil a day, roughly a fifth of the world's oil and a fifth of its LNG, moved through Hormuz before the war. Within hours of the 28 February strikes the IRGC radioed ships that no one would be allowed through. Iran never formally declared a blockade, but insurers withdrew cover, mines appeared from about 10 March, and attacks on tankers began on 1 March. The strait became, in the words used by shipping analysts, legally open but effectively closed.

This matters because it turned a regional air war into a global economic shock: Brent crossed 100 dollars on 8 March, Gulf producers cut output by at least 10 million barrels a day, the IEA released 400 million barrels, and around 20,000 seafarers and 2,000 ships were stranded. It also created a dual blockade: the US blocks Iran's exports while Iran blocks almost everyone else's.
year: 1 Mar: first tanker attacks (Skylight off Khasab, MKD Vyom by drone boat). 4 Mar: Iran claims 'complete control'; a sea drone hits the tanker Sonangol Namibe at a Kuwaiti port 800 km away. 6 Mar: UAE tug Mussafah 2 sunk by two missiles. ~10 Mar: first mines reported. 19 Mar: US launches an air campaign against Iranian boats; CENTCOM claims 130 vessels hit. 26 Mar: Iran lets ships of China, Russia, India, Iraq and Pakistan pass. 13 Apr: US blockade of Iran begins after Islamabad talks fail. 18 to 22 Apr: IRGC gunboats fire on ships and seize MSC Francesca and Epaminondas. 4 to 6 May: US Operation Project Freedom escorts ships out. 5 May: Iran creates the Persian Gulf Strait Authority to license transits and collect tolls. 17 Jun: Islamabad Memorandum lifts both blockades; oil falls to about 72 dollars. 8 Jul: three tankers hit near the Omani corridor; the US strikes 60 IRGC boats and the truce collapses. 12 Jul: IRGC declares the strait closed again. 14 Jul: three tankers hit in one morning; US blockade reinstated. Late July to August: Omani-Iranian talks on 'operational mechanisms' for passage; about 10 transits a day. 25 Aug: US says the shipping lanes are cleared of 100+ suspected mines. 30 Aug: US strikes Larak Island. 5 Sep: US disables Iranian tankers off Kharg, near Jask and in the Gulf of Oman. 6 Sep: Iran declares a prohibited zone up to the loading ports. October: two transits on 11 Oct; ships sunk near the strait; IRGC says two supertankers hit mines on an 'unauthorised route' around 22 Oct.
situation: As of late October 2026 Hormuz is closed to most traffic. Iran's permit system, toll demands and prohibited zone remain, and it says it is attacking ships that use unauthorised routes, including with mines. The US blockade of Iranian oil exports continues. UKMTO had logged 135 conflict-related incidents by 16 October and the maritime risk firm Marisks called October the most intense period since March. Brent was about 106 dollars in mid-October. Oman-Iran talks on joint management have produced no change in traffic.
technical: Iran never formally declared a blockade; closure was enforced by VHF warnings, insurance withdrawal and selective attacks, a cheap and deniable method.
Weapons used on ships: anti-ship and cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, one-way attack drones, explosive drone boats, sea mines, gunfire and rocket-propelled grenades from fast boats.
Sea mines were first reported around 10 March; by 25 August US underwater drones had found 100+ suspected mines in the Traffic Separation Scheme, cleared by private contractors.
GNSS spoofing and jamming across the strait complicated navigation and made ships stray into Iranian-claimed lanes.
Reach: an Iranian sea drone hit a tanker at Mubarak Al Kabeer port in Kuwait, more than 800 km from the strait; tankers were also hit off Basra, Ras Tanura, Ras Laffan, Dubai and Fujairah.
Iran's own corridor runs north of Larak Island; one ship reportedly paid 2 million dollars, with payments assessed in Chinese yuan (Lloyd's List).
Kpler counted 27 missile strikes in the strait between 6 July and early September 2026.
Traffic: about 85 transits a day before the war; around 10 a day in September; 2 on 11 October (IMF PortWatch).
Insurance: war-risk premiums went from 0.125% of hull value to 0.2 to 0.4% per transit, then 4 to 6 times higher by 9 March; P&I cover withdrawn from 5 March.
US blockade enforcement included seizures (15 ships by late July) and strikes; on 12 August a Panama-flagged ship that ignored warnings was hit by two Hellfire missiles near Pakistan.
US strikes on 8 July hit 60 IRGC small boats, coastal radars, surface-to-air and anti-ship missile sites, drone launch sites and port infrastructure at Sirik, Bandar Abbas and Qeshm.
India ran two naval escort operations, Sankalp (14 to 24 March) and Urja Suraksha (from 25 March, five-plus warships).

Prices: Brent passed 100 dollars on 8 March and peaked around 118 to 126 dollars; Dubai crude hit a record 166 dollars on 19 March; Brent fell to 71.57 dollars on 1 July, then rebounded to 106 dollars by mid-October.
casualties: Dozens of seafarers killed in attacks on merchant ships since 1 March 2026 (for example 2 on Skylight, 4 on the tug Mussafah 2, 3 on Mayuree Naree, 2 on Sidr, 1 on Hercules Star), many of them Indian nationals; IRGC Navy losses are not published (CENTCOM claims 130 vessels hit by 19 Mar and 60 boats on 8 Jul). No consolidated death toll was found (Wikipedia, 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis).
displaced: About 20,000 seafarers and 2,000 ships stranded inside the Gulf as of 21 April 2026 (IMO); 15,000 cruise passengers on six ships were stuck until about 18 April.

outlook: Watch whether Iran's mining of alternative routes near Oman continues, whether the US tries a forced escort or clearance operation after the midterms, and whether Oman-Iran talks yield a managed transit scheme acceptable to Washington. Any renewed US strikes would likely start with the IRGC Navy around Bandar Abbas, Qeshm and Jask.

battles.name: October 2026 mine and missile surge against shipping in Hormuz
battles.place: Strait of Hormuz, routes south of the strait (approximate)
sides: Merchant shipping using routes not authorised by Iran; US Navy
battles.outcome: IRGC says two supertankers hit mines on an 'unauthorised route' around 22 October, with engine-room fires; ships reported sunk near the strait in mid-October; US destroyed an Iranian-linked dhow in the Gulf of Oman on 6 October.
battles.forces: Naval mines, projectiles and drones; Iran also destroyed navigational aids.
battles.losses: Tanker and cargo ship losses; casualty figures not reported. UKMTO logged 135 conflict incidents by 16 October (CGTN).
battles.significance: Marisks called October the most intense month of maritime attacks since March; traffic fell to two transits on 11 October against 85 a day before the war.

sources.label: CGTN: Iran reports tanker blasts in Hormuz

battles.name: Iranian missile attack on a US carrier and US strikes on three Iranian tankers
battles.place: Off Kharg Island, near Jask and in the Gulf of Oman
sides: US Navy carrier strike group and CENTCOM
IRGC Aerospace Force and IRGC Navy
battles.outcome: The US carrier and destroyer evaded several Iranian ballistic missiles; CENTCOM disabled M/T Downy off Kharg and M/T Stark 1 near Jask and destroyed the empty M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman.
battles.forces: Several Iranian ballistic missiles; US strike aircraft.
battles.losses: Three Iranian crude carriers disabled or destroyed; no US casualties (CENTCOM via Times of Oman).
battles.significance: The first direct Iranian ballistic missile attack on a US carrier group in the war, and a US shift to destroying Iran's own tanker fleet.

sources.label: Times of Oman: IRGC says ballistic missiles fired at US carrier

battles.name: Triple tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz
sides: Tankers Stolt Magnesium, Mombasa B and Al Bahyah
battles.outcome: Three tankers hit in a single morning; the US reinstated its blockade of Iran.
battles.losses: 1 killed and 8 injured on Mombasa B; 3 crew missing from Al Bahyah (Wikipedia).
battles.significance: Confirmed the collapse of the June memorandum and opened a summer of missile attacks: Kpler counted 27 missile strikes in the strait from 6 July to early September.

battles.name: US air campaign against Iranian boats and drones in Hormuz
sides: US CENTCOM air and naval forces
IRGC Navy fast attack craft, mine-layers and drone units
battles.outcome: CENTCOM claimed 130 Iranian vessels struck by 19 March; Iran kept the strait closed regardless.
battles.forces: US carrier aircraft and land-based strike aircraft; Iran fielded 500 to 1,000+ fast boats (cited estimate).
battles.losses: 130 Iranian vessels claimed hit (CENTCOM via Wikipedia); a US A-10 was later shot down near the strait (3 April).
battles.significance: Showed that destroying boats did not reopen the strait, because mines, missiles and insurance withdrawal kept ships away.

battles.name: Sinking of the tug Mussafah 2
battles.place: Omani waters of the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab (approximate)
battles.outcome: Tug sunk by two missiles while helping the stricken tanker Safeen Prestige.
battles.losses: 4 crew killed (Wikipedia; one count says at least three missing).
battles.significance: Hitting a rescue tug signalled that even salvage and assistance vessels were fair game, deepening the shipping freeze.
